Insidious

in-SID-ee-us -- stress on the second syllable, SID. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Insidious is treacherous and subtly harmful; spreading damage gradually and stealthily.

The illness was insidious, quietly sapping her strength for months before the first clear symptom appeared.

Worked Example

A streaming app's autoplay feature starts the next episode before the credits finish, and a student who sat down for one twenty-minute show looks up to find the whole evening gone -- again.

That time-drain is insidious: the harm arrives so gradually and quietly that you never notice the moment it takes hold. Insidious dangers -- diseases, habits, influences -- do their damage before anyone thinks to look for them.

How Insidious Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

stealthy

stealthy: acting quietly and secretly to avoid notice

creeping

creeping: advancing slowly and almost imperceptibly

treacherous

treacherous: dangerous while appearing safe; betraying trust

Antonyms

harmless

harmless: causing no damage at all

overt

overt: done or shown openly, without concealment

How Strong Is It? — creeping → treacherous → insidious

creeping vs. insidious

creeping vs. insidious: Creeping notes only the slow, quiet advance -- a creeping vine climbs the wall harmlessly enough -- while insidious adds real damage waiting at the end of that quiet approach.

treacherous vs. insidious

treacherous vs. insidious: Treacherous raises the stakes past insidious: an insidious danger does its harm before you spot it, while a treacherous one betrays you outright, striking from the very place you trusted most.

Sort It Out

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: in, on, upon (not the negating in-) (Latin in-)

root — sid-/sed-

root — sid-/sed-: to sit (Latin sedere 'to sit'; insidiae 'an ambush')

suffix — -ious

suffix — -ious: full of; possessing the qualities of (Latin -osus, via Old French -ous)

Put it together

Put it together: Insidious uses the -ious variant of this unit's suffix family. Latin insidiae meant 'an ambush' -- from insidere, 'to sit in or upon,' because ambushers literally sit in wait. Something insidious is 'full of ambush': it settles in quietly, sits unnoticed, and springs its harm only after it has taken hold. Note that the in- here means 'in, on' -- not the negating in- you may remember from earlier morpheme study.

Word Choice

Insidious is for harm that spreads gradually and stays hidden: an insidious disease, an insidious habit, insidious propaganda. Keep this unit's three 'bad' words in their lanes -- insidious harm creeps in unseen, nefarious schemes are openly wicked and criminal, and egregious errors are shockingly bad in plain view.
